prompt.context: Our client is Magna Health, a health care company in the Midwest. It both insures patients and provides health care services. Employers pay a fixed premium to Magna for each of their employees in return for which Magna covers all necessary health services of the employee (ranging from physician care, and medications to hospitalization). Magna currently has 300,000 patients enrolled in its plan. It has 300 salaried physician employees who provide a broad range of services to patients in 6 centers. These physicians represent a wide range of specialty areas, but not all areas. When a patient needs medical treatment in a specialty area not covered by a Magna physician, they are referred outside of the Magna network for care, and Magna pays all referral costs on a fee-for-service basis. Magna doesn't own any hospitals itself, instead contracting services from several local hospitals. Over the past six months, Magna has been experiencing declining profitability. Magna's CEO has retained McKinsey to help determine what is causing the problem and how Magna might fix it.
prompt.question: How can Magna Health improve its financial situation?

clarifying_info.q: What are the prevalence rates of serious heart disease by age group?
clarifying_info.a: The prevalence rate of serious heart disease in the 65+ population is 30%; in the under-65 population it is 10%.

clarifying_info.q: How often do patients with serious heart disease visit cardiologists?
clarifying_info.a: In the U.S., patients with serious heart disease visit specialists (cardiologists) on average 5 times per year.

exhibits.title: Magna Health vs. Sunshine HMO: Patient and Referral Cost Comparison
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Magna Health and Sunshine HMO on two dimensions: number of patients and average cost of referral per member per month.

framework: Revenues: premium income per member, number of enrolled members, trends in enrollment
Costs — Administrative / Non-medical: overhead, staffing, facilities
Costs — Medical: hospital contracting costs, drug costs, outpatient care
Costs — Outpatient (drill down): internal physician costs vs. external referral costs
Patient demographics / risk profile: age distribution, disease prevalence, mix of referred specialties

questions.prompt: Question 1: What key areas would you want to explore in order to understand Magna's decline in profitability?
questions.guidance: A good answer covers revenues and costs (variable and fixed). Key cost components: administrative (non-medical) costs and medical costs (hospital, drugs, outpatient care). A very good answer further splits outpatient into internal physician costs vs. external referral costs, and also considers how patient demographics and overall risk profile affect medical costs.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Your team believes a root cause is the cost of referrals to specialists outside the physician network. Using the Exhibit 1 data, what are the most likely reasons Magna's average referral cost is higher than Sunshine's?
questions.guidance: Good answer: (1) Referral Pricing — Magna may be paying higher contracted rates for specialist services than Sunshine. (2) Number of referrals — Magna physicians may have different practice patterns (less comfortable treating certain conditions) leading to more referrals per patient. Very good answer adds: (3) Mix of specialties — Magna's referral specialties (cardiology, neurosurgery) are more expensive than Sunshine's (cardiology, psychiatry). (4) Mix of patients — Magna may have sicker or older (65+) patients who are more likely to need expensive specialist care.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Magna's CEO asks how many cardiology referrals should be expected annually based on its patient population. Assume: 300,000 total patients, 20% aged 65+, serious heart disease prevalence 30% in 65+ and 10% in under-65, cardiologist visits average 5 per year per patient with serious heart disease.
questions.guidance: Segment the population into 65+ and under-65, apply prevalence rates, then multiply by visit frequency. Expected answer: 210,000 annual cardiac referrals.

math.setup: Segment patients by age, apply disease prevalence rate to each segment, then multiply by 5 visits/year.
steps: 60,000 x 30% prevalence = 18,000 patients with serious heart disease
240,000 x 10% prevalence = 24,000 patients with serious heart disease
24,000 x 5 visits = 120,000 referrals from under-65 group

questions.prompt: Question 4: The CEO reveals Magna currently pays for 300,000 annual cardiology referrals — far above the 210,000 expected. Why might Magna's actual referrals be significantly higher than U.S. averages?
questions.guidance: Good answer: The prevalence rate of heart disease in Magna's patient population is higher than the U.S. average. Follow-on: Why would a physician refer a patient who does not have serious heart disease to a specialist? Good answer: patients are demanding referrals. Very good answer adds: (1) Primary care physicians are poorly trained or inexperienced with cardiac patients and fear malpractice suits. (2) Magna lacks clear referral guidelines, or physicians are not complying with existing ones. (3) No incentives or penalties to prevent over-referral.

questions.prompt: Question 5A: The team proposes a physician incentive pilot: $1M in overall fee increases to primary care physicians + $100,000 bonuses to each of the 10 primary care physicians with the lowest cardiac referral rates (consistent with good outcomes). How many fewer cardiology referrals must Magna achieve to recoup the cost of the pilot? Assume cost per referral = $200 and current annual referrals = 300,000.
questions.guidance: Calculate total pilot cost, then divide by cost per referral to get required referral reduction; express as a percentage. Answer: 10,000 fewer referrals (3.3% reduction) breaks even.

math.setup: Total incentive cost divided by cost per referral equals number of referrals that must be eliminated.
math.answer: Magna needs to reduce referrals by 10,000 (3.3%) to recoup the pilot cost.

questions.prompt: Question 5B: The team projects the incentive plan will reduce referrals by 5% in Year 1 and an additional 2% in Year 2. How much total referral cost could Magna save over the two years?
questions.guidance: Apply Year 1 reduction to base, calculate savings. Apply Year 2 reduction to the new lower base, calculate savings. Sum both years. Answer: $7.14M total over two years.

math.setup: Year 1 reduction applied to 300,000 baseline; Year 2 reduction applied to the post-Year-1 baseline of 285,000.
steps: Year 1: 5% x 300,000 = 15,000 fewer referrals; 15,000 x $200 = $3.0M saved
Year 2: 2% x 285,000 = 5,700 fewer referrals; 5,700 x $200 = $1.14M saved
math.answer: $7.14M in total referral cost savings over two years.

questions.prompt: Question 6 (Brainstorm): Beyond cardiac financial incentive programs, what other ideas should Magna consider to reduce the cost of specialist referrals?
questions.guidance: Good answer focuses on additional ways to change physician behavior. Very good answer also raises ideas outside physician behavior change.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond cardiac financial incentive programs, what other ideas should Magna consider to reduce the cost of specialist referrals?

categories.name: Change Physician Behavior (non-financial)
ideas: Provide training on how to treat patients with minor or stable medical problems
Define and clarify medical guidelines for referrals (e.g., establish a medical committee to define the difference between 'serious' and 'minor' heart disease)
Institute a peer review committee charged with approving a subset of referrals (e.g., those considered high-cost)

categories.name: Identify Outliers
ideas: Investigate 'outlier' physicians who refer at much higher rates than peers to determine whether focusing on a few physicians will dramatically reduce referral costs

categories.name: Other Cost Levers
ideas: Renegotiate contract rates with specialist providers to reduce cost per referral
Bring high-volume specialty areas (e.g., cardiology) in-house to convert fee-for-service costs to fixed costs
Improve patient triage and care management to address disease risk before specialist referral becomes necessary

recommendation: Implement the overall fee increase pilot ($1M) to incentivize primary care physicians to handle more basic cardiology needs in-house
Evaluate the bonus plan ($100K x 10 physicians) with careful attention to ethical implications of incentivizing non-referral
Establish clear referral guidelines and a peer review committee to govern when referrals are appropriate
Train primary care physicians on managing minor cardiac conditions to reduce unnecessary referrals
Investigate high-referral outlier physicians to target intervention efforts efficiently
risks: Ethical risk: financial incentives may discourage appropriate referrals, harming patient outcomes
Patient resistance: patients may demand specialist access and push back against new referral controls
Physician resistance: salaried physicians may resist monitoring or guideline constraints
Guideline implementation may be slow and inconsistent across the 6 centers
next_steps: Launch and measure the physician fee increase pilot and track referral rate changes
Convene a medical committee to draft evidence-based referral guidelines within 90 days
Analyze referral data by physician to identify and engage outliers
Assess feasibility and cost-benefit of bringing cardiology in-house given referral volume
